name: Mycenaean Greece (palatial kingdoms)

areaKm2.note: Educated guess. High = historical-basemaps world_bc1500 'Greek city-states' polygon (mainland Greece, Crete and Aegean islands; nearest file at or before 1250) computed from the GeoJSON at ~141,000 km2. The palatial territories proper (Argolid, Messenia, Laconia, Boeotia, Attica, southern Thessaly, Crete) covered less.

population.note: OWID historical population (https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/population.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true): Greece 0.3 M in 2000 BCE and 1.0 M in 1000 BCE; linear interpolation gives ~0.83 M at 1250, but the Late Bronze Age peak was followed by collapse, so the curve is not linear; Seshat codes Mycenaean Crete (Monopalatial) at 50,000-80,000 (https://seshat-db.com/core/polity/63). Mid is a judgement within the range.

urbanization.note: Educated guess. Palatial centres of a few thousand to ~10,000 (Seshat codes Knossos at ~10,000).

activePersonnel.note: Educated guess. No Mycenaean army total exists. Anchors: the Pylos rower tablets list ~600 rowers called up by one kingdom, enough for 12-30 ships (Wachsmann 1999, fetched); the Pylos o-ka tablets assign small coastal detachments; every rural community (damos) owed men (D'Amato and Salimbeti 2011, cited in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece). Sum over ~6-10 palatial states (Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos, Thebes, Orchomenos/Gla, Athens, Knossos, Iolkos).

trainedReserves.note: Educated guess. Damos levies callable in a month.

supportPersonnel.note: Educated guess. Rowers and chariot crews in service at a given time; the Pylos call-up of ~600 rowers in one kingdom scaled to all palaces.

mobilizationRatio.note: Educated guess. Palace-administered service from every damos.

mobilizable.note: population x mobilizationRatio (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

count.note: Educated guess. No Mycenaean army total exists. Anchors: the Pylos rower tablets list ~600 rowers called up by one kingdom, enough for 12-30 ships (Wachsmann 1999, fetched); the Pylos o-ka tablets assign small coastal detachments; every rural community (damos) owed men (D'Amato and Salimbeti 2011, cited in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece). Sum over ~6-10 palatial states (Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos, Thebes, Orchomenos/Gla, Athens, Knossos, Iolkos). Split: close-order spearmen ~60% of the foot.

quality.note: Bronze spears, swords, boar's tusk and bronze helmets, figure-of-eight and round shields; most hoplite-panoply elements already present (Kagan and Viggiano via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece).

count.note: Educated guess. No Mycenaean army total exists. Anchors: the Pylos rower tablets list ~600 rowers called up by one kingdom, enough for 12-30 ships (Wachsmann 1999, fetched); the Pylos o-ka tablets assign small coastal detachments; every rural community (damos) owed men (D'Amato and Salimbeti 2011, cited in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece). Sum over ~6-10 palatial states (Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos, Thebes, Orchomenos/Gla, Athens, Knossos, Iolkos). Split: archers and slingers ~15% of the foot.

Educated guess. No Mycenaean army total exists. Anchors: the Pylos rower tablets list ~600 rowers called up by one kingdom, enough for 12-30 ships (Wachsmann 1999, fetched); the Pylos o-ka tablets assign small coastal detachments; every rural community (damos) owed men (D'Amato and Salimbeti 2011, cited in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece). Sum over ~6-10 palatial states (Mycenae, Tiryns, Pylos, Thebes, Orchomenos/Gla, Athens, Knossos, Iolkos). Split: javelin skirmishers ~25% of the foot.

Educated guess. Knossos Linear B chariot tablets inventory chariots, horses and corslets in the low hundreds for Crete alone; Pylos tablets record chariot wheels. By the 13th century chariots served mainly as battlefield transport (Fields 2004, cited in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycenaean_Greece). Crews in supportPersonnel.

quality.note: Light rail chariot; used as transport more than as an archery platform.

count.note: Wachsmann 1999: the Pylos An 610 tablet lists ~600 rowers, sufficient for thirty 20-oared ships, twenty triaconters or twelve penteconters, for one kingdom. Scaled to all Aegean palaces. Homer's Catalogue of 1,186 ships is not used.

quality.note: Oared galleys (penteconter-type), the leading warship of the late Bronze Age Aegean.

commandQuality.note: Rubric 0.5: palace bureaucracies organised supply and call-ups; no unified command across kingdoms.

cohesion.note: Rubric 0.25-0.5: separate palace states, aristocratic retinues.

morale.note: Rubric 0.5: average; pressure that preceded the c. 1200 collapse.

weapons.note: Anchor 2: bronze swords and spears, chariots, composite bows rare.

armor.note: Anchor 2+: Dendra-type bronze plate panoply (earlier), boar's tusk and bronze helmets.

ships.note: Anchor 2+: oared galleys, strong naval tradition.

fortification.note: Above anchor 2: Cyclopean citadels (Mycenae, Tiryns, Gla, Athens) with hidden cisterns.

logistics.note: Below 2: palace store-rooms, engineered roads with culverts and bridges in the Argolid; small kingdoms.

communications.note: Below 2: palace couriers; beacon chains plausible.

gdpPerCapita.note: Maddison Project 2023 via https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/gdp-per-capita-maddison-project-database.csv?v=1&csvType=full&useColumnShortNames=true: Greece 1 CE = 1,275 (2011 int$). Late Bronze Age palatial economy scaled down by about a third.

gdp.note: population x gdpPerCapita (low x low, mid x mid, high x high).

milSpendShare.note: Educated guess. Heavy palace investment in fortifications and bronze armour.

industrialShare.note: Educated guess. Palace-controlled craft production (textiles, perfumed oil, bronze).

foodSurplus.note: Educated guess. Mediterranean dry farming; palace stores redistributed grain.

annualCohort.note: population x 0.0095: Hansen 2006 (https://ancientportsantiques.com/wp-content/uploads/Documents/PLACES/GreeceContinental/Athens-Hansen2006.pdf, p. 34) puts a year class of 18-19-year-olds at ca. 1.9% of all males in a pre-modern age structure, i.e. ~0.95% of total population reaching military age per year (males only). Same model as the classical snapshots; Bronze Age life expectancy was if anything lower, so this is not an underestimate.

roadKm.note: Educated guess. Engineered Mycenaean roads with culverts and bridges (e.g. Arkadiko bridge) in the Argolid and around other palaces.

majorPorts.note: Educated guess. Nauplion/Tiryns, Pylos, Iolkos, Knossos/Amnisos, Piraeus area, island harbours.

merchantTonnage.note: Educated guess. Merchant ships of 10-20 t (Uluburun-type) trading to Cyprus, Egypt, the Levant.

supplyRangeKm.note: Educated guess. Short-range armies in a mountainous peninsula; sea transport for longer moves.

draftAnimals.note: Educated guess. Oxen, donkeys, horses; ~0.1-0.17 per inhabitant.

homeDefense.note: Rubric 1.2: mountain terrain and Cyclopean citadels; no deep strategic depth.

notes: Snapshot = c. 1250 BCE, LH IIIB palatial peak (Ahhiyawa of the Hittite texts). Mycenaean Greece was a set of palace kingdoms, not one state; this snapshot aggregates them, so commandQuality and cohesion are low. Capital = Mycenae as the leading centre. All force numbers are reconstructions from Linear B (Pylos rower and o-ka tablets, Knossos chariot tablets) and are grade D; Homer is not used. Population convention: mainland palatial regions, Crete and the Aegean inside the border.
